definition.text: Diversification is spreading money across different investments so that no single asset or risk can do too much harm.

facts.text: The proverb 'don't put all your eggs in one basket' sums it up: more risk of losing one egg, less of losing them all.
If prices do not move in perfect step, a diversified portfolio varies less than the average of its parts.
It narrows the range of outcomes: returns never beat the best single asset nor fall below the worst.
Holding just one stock is risky; a single stock can fall 50% in a year.
A 1977 study found 30 stocks gave almost the same risk reduction as 1,000, and even four gave most of it.
Market correlations tend to rise in crises, weakening diversification just when investors need it.

definition.text: Diversifiable risk comes from a single company and can be spread away; systematic, or market, risk affects all assets and cannot.

facts.text: Buying all S&P 500 stocks leaves only the risk of index moves, while one stock also carries company-specific risk.
The company-specific part shrinks as more stocks are held, which is why it is called diversifiable.

definition.text: Mixing assets can bring a portfolio's variance, a measure of risk, below that of even its least risky asset.

facts.text: With fraction q in asset X and 1-q in uncorrelated asset Y, portfolio variance is q²σx² + (1-q)²σy².
Variance is lowest at q = σy²/(σx²+σy²), giving σx²σy²/(σx²+σy²), below either asset held alone.
Markowitz's 1952 mean-variance framework showed portfolio risk depends on the covariance among returns, not just each asset's variance.

definition.text: Stock is all the shares into which ownership of a company is divided; one share is a fraction of ownership.

facts.text: A share usually entitles its holder to part of the company's earnings, part of what is left after debts in liquidation, and votes.
Common stock usually carries votes; preferred stock usually does not but gets dividends first.
Selling shares to the public on a stock exchange for the first time is an initial public offering, or IPO.
Raising money by selling stock is equity financing, while issuing bonds is debt financing that avoids giving up ownership.
A share's price at any moment is set by supply and demand for it.
Shareholders' claims on company assets rank below those of creditors.

definition.text: Eco-investing, or green investing, is socially responsible investing focused on companies that offer environmentally friendly products and practices.

facts.text: Unlike broader socially responsible investing, it narrows to environmental issues, especially renewable energy and clean technology.
One tracker estimated over $1.248 trillion invested in solar, wind, geothermal, ocean and other green sectors since 2007.
New green technologies carry high up-front costs that are harder to justify to investors.
